       5. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK   Computational journalist Brian Whitton: In the early spring, I got together with my colleagues on the data team to answer a key question driving our midterms coverage: What could online conversations tell us about what voters care about ahead of the election?

   We spent the next several months building an AI tool that consumes content from across the digital world. It worked a little too well. We’ve got thousands of hours of cable news broadcasts, a quarter million podcast episodes and over 11 million TikToks.

   Making sense of it all is a challenge. We’ve spent endless hours reading transcripts and watching hours of TikToks to fact-check the tool’s findings.

   One thing we’re interested in is how nonpolitical ideas are characterized in political spaces. We think there’s more to say about how ideology and politics move through spaces we haven’t traditionally had a pulse on.

   We’re planning a series of reports based on what the tool surfaces between now and Election Day. This first dispatch focused on podcasts, and how the conversation among Trump’s most vocal supporters has changed since the 2024 election, when MAGA podcasts really set the agenda.

Flow of Chinese Components to Iran Shadows Trump’s Summit With Xi

BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

This summer, when the U.S. and Iran signed a temporary truce, China touted its role in easing tensions in the Middle East. That same day, a plane from China landed in Tehran carrying electronics components that can be used to make parts for drones and missile guidance systems, according to Iranian customs data analyzed by the Journal.

 

Two days later, there were more than a dozen other shipments carrying parts worth more than $6 million that can be used in drones. Chinese entities have made thousands of shipments of such “dual use” tech. 

 

Chinese leader Xi Jinping is visiting President Trump in Washington this week for a summit covering weighty topics including trade, artificial intelligence and Taiwan. But the elephant in the room will be China’s continuing support for Iran.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

5. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK

 

Computational journalist Brian Whitton: In the early spring, I got together with my colleagues on the data team to answer a key question driving our midterms coverage: What could online conversations tell us about what voters care about ahead of the election?

 

We spent the next several months building an AI tool that consumes content from across the digital world. It worked a little too well. We’ve got thousands of hours of cable news broadcasts, a quarter million podcast episodes and over 11 million TikToks.

 

Making sense of it all is a challenge. We’ve spent endless hours reading transcripts and watching hours of TikToks to fact-check the tool’s findings.

 

One thing we’re interested in is how nonpolitical ideas are characterized in political spaces. We think there’s more to say about how ideology and politics move through spaces we haven’t traditionally had a pulse on.

 

We’re planning a series of reports based on what the tool surfaces between now and Election Day. This first dispatch focused on podcasts, and how the conversation among Trump’s most vocal supporters has changed since the 2024 election, when MAGA podcasts really set the agenda.

 

One of the biggest surprises to us was also the most basic: The tool actually worked. It made it easy to click around and find ordinary creators posting political content. 6. SEE THE STORY

 

Here’s how Elon Musk’s Sunbelt investments are reshaping his business empire.

 
 
MERRILL SHERMAN
 

More than 20 years after Musk got his start in California, the serial entrepreneur has expanded his empire with infrastructure projects across the southern half of the U.S. This year alone, Tesla and SpaceX have announced billions of dollars in new projects in Texas and Louisiana. States are racing to offer lucrative tax-incentive packages to win new business from Musk’s companies and, in some cases, introducing laws that make it easier for the companies to operate.
